cur:manuscripts-stuttgart-psalter-psalm-.summary: Beneath the verse 'the kings of Tharsis and of the isles shall bring presents: the kings of Arabia and of Saba shall bring gifts', the Virgin sits enthroned under an arch holding the Christ Child, as the three Magi approach with their gifts beneath a shining star.
facts: The Stuttgart Psalter was made around 820–830 at the abbey of Saint-Germain-des-Prés near Paris; its 168 leaves contain the psalms with 316 coloured miniatures set between the verses they illustrate.
Its pictures interpret the psalms literally, historically or — very often — Christologically, as prophecies of the life of Christ.
cur:manuscripts-stuttgart-psalter-psalm-.notes: Image from the WLB digital facsimile (Public Domain Mark), showing the whole page with the miniature.

europeana:9200579/sydj252z.summary: Christ stands in a sunlit clearing at the centre of a gathered crowd of men, women and children, one hand open in a gesture of teaching. At the left a woman kneels beside a clump of flowers, and the Wellcome Collection explains that he is pointing to Mary with the lilies as he speaks the words 'Consider the lilies how they grow'. The calm, balanced composition, framed by an ornamental border, carries Julius Hübner's devotional painting to a wide Victorian-era public.
facts: Julius Hübner (1806–1882), a history painter of the Düsseldorf school, painted a 'Consider the Lilies' in 1839; this lithograph reproduces his composition.

The print was drawn on the stone by Christian Georg Hahn and published in Berlin by L. Sachse, with Goupil & Vibert in Paris and Hering & Remington in London as co-publishers, showing how such religious images circulated internationally.
It is a large sheet: image, lettering and border measure about 52 × 69.5 cm (Wellcome Collection 766646i).
europeana:9200579/sydj252z.notes: Wellcome dates the print '[between 1840 and 1849?]'; our date '184X'/year 184 was a parsing error. The Wellcome record has been merged into work gb3h2bx7.

vam:O72543.summary: Christ hangs on the cross at the centre of this Metz ivory, with angels on either side waiting to receive his soul and busts of the Sun and Moon above. To his right stand the Virgin and Ecclesia, the Church, holding a chalice to catch his blood; to his left St John and Synagoga with her banner. Longinus and Stephaton stand below, the dead emerge from round mausolea, and large figures of Earth and Water recline at the base — a whole theology of redemption gathered around the cross.
facts: The V&A explains the symbolism: the serpent at the foot of the cross is sin overcome by Christ, Ecclesia's chalice refers to the Eucharist, and the rising dead show the conquest of death.
The surface is dotted with holes that once held gold studs, a few of which survive.
The relief was once believed to come from a Gospel-book cover in Verdun Cathedral, but the V&A now rejects this, suggesting that the Verdun cover held a virtually identical plaque.
